Part 1

What hydrology is

Definitions, surface water vs. groundwater, and where hydrology sits among the earth sciences

What is hydrology?

Key idea

Hydrology is the science that describes and predicts the occurrence, circulation and distribution of Earth's water.

Hydrology studies the quantity and movement of water resources on the planet, or the lack of water.

Two extremes

  • A lack of water can cause drought
  • An excess of water can cause flooding

What controls where water is

  • Weather is the biggest influence on the movement and availability of water over the planet
  • Regional geography and humans play a smaller role in the spatial distribution of water

Hydrology: a formal definition

Key idea

Hydrology means “the knowledge of water”: from Greek hydro (hudor, water) and Latin -logy (logia, knowledge).

The classic definition

“Hydrology is the science that treats the waters of the Earth, their occurrence, circulation, and distribution, their chemical and physical properties, and their reaction with their environment, including their relation to living things. The domain of hydrology embraces the full life history of water on the Earth.”

Ad Hoc Panel on Hydrology (1962), Scientific Hydrology

Pure and applied science

Earth science perspective (our focus) vs. engineering perspective

Surface water

Above-ground water. Most of this course, with a focus on rivers and streams.

Groundwater

Below-surface water. We cover soil water only; groundwater hydrology is a full course in civil engineering.

Scope of hydrology

Key idea

Water is one of the most valuable natural resources, essential for human and animal life, industry and agriculture.

Water is also used for

  • Power generation
  • Navigation
  • Fisheries

Why hydrology gets so much attention

Around the world, hydrology underpins the development and management of water resources for:

  • Irrigation and water supply
  • Flood control
  • Water-logging and salinity control
  • Hydropower and navigation

Hydrology and other earth and environmental sciences

Key idea

Hydrology sits at the center of the earth sciences: where it overlaps a neighbor, an interdisciplinary field appears.

Read the figure

Each circle is a neighboring science. The labels at the sides name the field where it meets hydrology:

  • Geomorphology → fluvial geomorphology
  • Ecology → ecohydrology, hydroecology
  • Geology → groundwater hydrology
  • Climatology / meteorology → hydroclimatology, hydrometeorology

Reflect

Where do you see yourself belonging? Which overlap is closest to your own interests or project?

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q1 Define hydrology in one sentence. What three aspects of Earth's water does it describe?

The science that describes and predicts Earth's water: its occurrence, circulation and distribution (and, in the full definition, its properties and interactions with the environment).

Q2 What are the two main types of hydrology, and which one is the focus of this course?

Surface water (above ground) and groundwater (below ground). This course focuses on surface water, especially rivers and streams, plus soil water.

Q3 Name the field where hydrology overlaps with ecology, and the one where it overlaps with geology.

Ecology: ecohydrology / hydroecology. Geology: groundwater hydrology.

Part 2

Why hydrology matters

Water concerns, 21st-century challenges, and how we manage water

Why study hydrology?

Key idea

The better we understand water, the better we can manage it around the globe.

  • We are dealing with one of Earth's most valuable resources
  • Hydrology explains how water interacts with its environment, including how it moves from Earth's surface to the atmosphere and back
  • It covers the natural distribution and movement of water, and also the impact of human activities on water quality and problems in water management
  • Many industries have a great need for water. In agriculture, water irrigates farmland and supports livestock

Hydrology concerns

Key idea

Hydrologists work on water quality and quantity across natural, agricultural, urban and recreational settings.

Too much or too little water in the “wrong places”

Key idea

Water problems are often about distribution: the water is not where people need it, or it arrives all at once.

Too little

Worldwide, about a third of children are malnourished, and more than one billion people lack safe water to drink.

Too much

Water-related hazards dominate the list of disasters in both human and economic toll over the past 50 years.

Population growth and water demand

Key idea

Every minute the population of the world increases by about 200 people, and each needs water from a finite supply.

Read the graph

  • World population (billions) rises steadily from about 3 billion in 1960 toward about 9 billion by 2050
  • The annual increase (%) falls over the same period

So growth is slowing in percentage terms, but the total number of people, and the water they need, keeps climbing.

Water and conflict

Key idea

Water may become the most important resource countries fight over in the late 21st century.

Read the map

Each dot is a recorded water conflict (3000 BC – 2019 AD, Pacific Institute Water Conflict Chronology). Colors show the role water played:

  • Water as a casualty of conflict
  • Water as a trigger or root cause
  • Water as a weapon

Blue Gold

The poster is from Blue Gold: World Water Wars, a documentary about the coming “war over water.”

Water topics in the 21st century

Key idea

Towards a sustainable future: four connected water topics.

Climate change

Changes where, when and how much water is available.

Hydropolitics

Who controls shared water, and how it is negotiated.

Desalination

Turning seawater into fresh water.

Water scarcity

Places where demand exceeds available supply.

Three major themes in hydrology for the 21st century

Key idea

Three questions drive modern hydrology: is our water use sustainable, how is the system changing, and how do we manage it globally?

Sustainability

Quantifying the sustainability of water resources, waste management and environmental systems.

Change

Quantifying hydrological change arising from modification to the climate, land use and management of environmental systems.

The global environment

Evaluation and management of the global environment through remote sensing, environmental modeling and hazard reduction.

Management perspectives

Key idea

A water right is the right to use water, not ownership of the water itself.

Can we control water? Who should control it?

  • Water rights: a legal entitlement authorizing water to be diverted from a specified source and put to beneficial, nonwasteful use. Water rights are property rights
  • Water management: controlling the movement of water to minimize damage to life and property and maximize efficient beneficial use

Too much or too little water?

  • Diversion: pipes and canals
  • Storage: dams, reservoirs, water towers

Keeping water quality good

Source water protection, pollution prevention, treatment and remediation, and active monitoring

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q4 Give two examples of “too much” and “too little” water problems.

Too little: drought, lack of safe drinking water, malnutrition. Too much: floods and other water-related disasters, which dominate the human and economic toll of disasters.

Q5 What do the three 21st-century themes in hydrology have in common?

All three are about quantifying and managing water systems at large scales: sustainability, change (climate, land use) and the global environment (remote sensing, modeling, hazard reduction).

Q6 Does a water-right holder own the water? Explain.

No. A water right is a property right to use water (divert it from a source for beneficial, nonwasteful use), not ownership of the water itself.

Part 3

Earth's water and the water cycle

Where Earth's water is stored, how it moves, and the water budget

Where is Earth's water?

Key idea

We are surrounded by water, but only a very small percentage of it is available to us.

Read the bars from left to right

  • Total water: oceans 96.5%, other saline water 0.9%, freshwater only 2.5%
  • Freshwater: glaciers and ice caps 68.7%, groundwater 30.1%, surface and other 1.2%
  • Surface and other freshwater: ground ice and permafrost 69%, lakes 20.9%, soil moisture 3.8%, atmosphere 3.0%, swamps 2.6%, rivers 0.49%, living things 0.26%

Rivers, the water we see most, hold under half a percent of a percent of all water.

The hydrological (water) cycle

Key idea

The water cycle is the continuous movement and change of phase of water between ocean, atmosphere and land.

  • You will find many versions of the water cycle, depending on the system it represents
  • It typically involves physical movement and change of phase of water
  • The water cycle shapes landscapes, transports minerals, and is essential to most life and ecosystems on the planet

Following water around the cycle

Key idea

Trace one path around the figure: ocean → atmosphere → land → back to ocean.

1. The ocean holds about 97% of Earth's water

2. Heat from the sun causes water to evaporate

3. Water vapor rises and condenses as clouds

4. Winds move clouds through the atmosphere

5. Droplets fall as drizzle, rain, snow or ice

6. Snow and ice accumulate, then melt to liquid or turn to vapor

7. Water flows above ground as runoff, forming streams, rivers, swamps, ponds and lakes

8. Plants take up water and transpire it back into the air

9. Water infiltrates, flows underground, and seeps back out enriched in minerals

10. Water penetrating Earth's crust can return as geysers or volcanic steam

The water budget

Key idea

P − E − R = ΔS: precipitation minus evaporation minus runoff equals the change in storage.

Some call it the water balance equation.

Terms

  • P: precipitation (into the basin)
  • E: evaporation, or evapotranspiration (out of the basin)
  • R: runoff (out of the basin)
  • ΔS: change in storage, in soil or bedrock

Read the figure

The basin is a container. P adds water, E and R remove it, and whatever is left over changes S.

To keep things simple, this course mainly uses this basic form.

The water budget depends on the system

Key idea

The water balance equation is different for each system: groundwater, soil water and reservoirs each have their own form.

Basic form (our focus)

P − E − R = ΔS

Precipitation in; evaporation and runoff out.

A more detailed form

P + I = ET + Inf + R + ΔS

  • In: P precipitation (incl. snow), I irrigation
  • Out: ET evapotranspiration, Inf infiltration, R surface runoff or drainage
  • ΔS: change in water storage

Soil water balance

ΔS = P − DS − RO − ET − D

  • ΔS: change in soil storage
  • DS: deep seepage
  • RO: surface runoff
  • ET: evapotranspiration
  • D: artificial drainage

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q7 What percentage of Earth's water is freshwater, and where is most of that freshwater stored?

About 2.5%. Most of it (68.7%) is in glaciers and ice caps; another 30.1% is groundwater.

Q8 Name four processes in the water cycle that involve a change of phase.

Any four of: evaporation, condensation, melting, sublimation (ice to vapor), freezing, and transpiration (liquid water in plants to vapor).

Q9 A basin receives 900 mm of precipitation in a year, loses 500 mm to evaporation and 300 mm to runoff. What is ΔS, and what does its sign mean?

ΔS = 900 − 500 − 300 = +100 mm. Positive, so storage in the basin increased that year.

Part 4

Watersheds and hydrologic units

How land is divided into drainage areas, from local creeks to national regions

Catchment, basin, watershed

Key idea

A watershed is an area of land that drains all its streams and rainfall to a common outlet.

The outlet can be the outflow of a reservoir, the mouth of a bay, or any point along a stream channel.

Read the figure

  • Watershed boundary along the ridges at the top
  • Headwaters and tributaries join to form the main stream
  • Wetlands, floodplain and streambank along the channel
  • Water table and groundwater below the surface

What is a watershed? The leaf analogy

Key idea

Think of a watershed as a leaf: the edge is the boundary and the veins are the streams.

The analogy

  • Leaf edge = watershed boundary
  • Veins = streams and creeks
  • Central vein = the main stream, carrying water to a larger river, lake, bay or ocean

The watershed divide

A ridge of high ground. Precipitation on one side drains into one watershed; on the other side, into a different one.

Watersheds are made of sub-basins, and they include both surface water and groundwater.

Watersheds near Portland and across Oregon

Key idea

Watersheds nest: Portland's local creeks drain to the Willamette and Columbia, which belong to Oregon's large basins.

Portland watersheds

Columbia Slough, Willamette River, Johnson Creek, Fanno Creek and Tryon Creek

Oregon's basins

Includes the North, Mid and South Coast, Willamette, Sandy, Hood, Deschutes, John Day, Umatilla, Grande Ronde, Powder, Malheur, Owyhee, Malheur Lake, Goose & Summer Lakes, Klamath, Rogue and Umpqua

Try it

Which of these basins do you live in?

Beautifully mapped watersheds in the United States

Key idea

Every stream in the country belongs to a watershed. Colors show the major river basins.

Find your own watershed

The USGS StreamStats tool lets you delineate the watershed boundary of any point you click, and shows information about that watershed.

Try it

Click your home or a nearby stream and delineate the area that drains to it.

Hydrologic unit maps

Key idea

The U.S. is divided into nested hydrologic units, each with a unique hydrologic unit code (HUC).

  • Units are nested from largest to smallest: regions → subregions → accounting units → cataloging units
  • Each unit's code has 2 to 8 digits, two digits per level
  • Left: the 21 water resource regions. Right: the same regions by name

The current national Watershed Boundary Dataset continues the nesting to 12-digit units (see Lecture 3a).

Try it

Find and locate your watershed. What is the name of your home's watershed?

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q10 What defines a watershed?

All the land that drains its streams and rainfall to a common outlet (a reservoir outflow, a bay mouth, or any point on a stream).

Q11 In the leaf analogy, what does the edge of the leaf represent, and what does the central vein represent?

The edge is the watershed boundary (divide); the central vein is the main stream carrying water to the outlet.

Q12 How many digits does a cataloging unit code have in the four-level HUC system?

8 digits (2 for the region, plus 2 for each smaller level).

Part 5

Thinking like a hydrologist

Space and time scales, geographic perspectives, complex systems and careers

Hydrology in space and time

Key idea

Water events happen over very different time intervals and areas. Always ask: how big, and how long?

Read the figures

Both plot length against time scale. Match your data and methods to the scale of the process.

Small and fast

Infiltration, urban drainage, convective storm cells: minutes to hours, meters to kilometers.

Large and slow

Groundwater aquifers, drought, drainage network formation: years to millennia, hundreds of kilometers.

Four geographic perspectives of hydrology

1. Location

Spatial distribution of water: how much water is at a specific location, within a specific area

2. Movement

Where is the water coming from?

Where is the water going?

3. Scale

Global, regional, local

Macro vs. micro

4. Human–environment interactions

Agent of diverse landforms

Changes in water quality

Community vulnerability to environmental change

Water as a complex environmental system

Key idea

Water is linked to energy and food: change one, and the others respond.

“All human and natural systems are influenced by the distribution, abundance, quality and accessibility of water… Integrated, multi-disciplinary, and multi-scale water-related research is necessary for meeting the challenge.”

“The results could then be applied to other potential focus areas for research on complex environmental systems, such as land use, energy and climate.”

Read the figure

The water–energy–food (WEF) nexus. Outside pressures include climate change, population growth and governability.

Careers in hydrology

Geoscientists and hydrologists

Geoscientist, hydrologist, hydrogeologist, water resource specialist, atmospheric scientist, oceanographer

Engineers

Civil, environmental, water resource, marine, mechanical, mining and geological engineers

Water and waste treatment

Plant operators

Environmental science technicians

Hydrologic technicians, GIS analysts

Biological scientists

Biological scientist, environmental scientist, environmental specialist

Utilities

Power plant operators, distributors, dispatchers, engineers

Consulting services

Consultants, watershed managers, project managers, water rights coordinators

Academic

Researchers, teachers and professors

Employers

Architecture, engineering, consulting and science firms; governments; universities and schools; research labs

Q13 Give one hydrologic process that is small and fast and one that is large and slow.

Small and fast: infiltration, urban drainage, a convective storm cell. Large and slow: groundwater flow in aquifers, drought, formation of drainage networks.

Q14 List the four geographic perspectives of hydrology.

Location, movement, scale, and human–environment interactions.

Q15 What is the WEF nexus, and why does it matter for water research?

The water–energy–food nexus: the three systems depend on each other (e.g., water for hydropower and irrigation, energy for treatment and pumping), so water research must be integrated and multi-disciplinary.
